newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE tells Albania to reach poll deal by midnight.
newsitem.headline: OSCE tells Albania to reach poll deal by midnight.

text.p: European envoy Franz Vranitzky on Tuesday gave Albania's squabbling politicians until the end of the day to reach a deal on an election law, warning that their country's future depended on them reaching a compromise.

"Time is running out. The government of national reconciliation, the prime minister and the president must reach agreement today," Vranitzky said in a statement after holding talks on Albania with U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan.

Annan, on a visit to Vienna, also urged President Sali Berisha, Prime Minister Bashkim Fino and other political leaders to reach an accord quickly, saying preparations for a free and fair election planned for June 29 had to go ahead.
"The parties must understand that they have to strike a compromise in order to reach an agreement," he told reporters.

Vranitzky, heading a mission to Albania on behalf of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), has travelled to Tirana several times to try to smooth the differences between Berisha's rightist Democrats, who dominate parliament, and opposition parties, led by the Socialists.
"Albania's prospects for the future and its place within the international community hinge on its ability to implement its commitments," the former Austrian chancellor said.
Vranitzky was due to address the OSCE's Vienna-based permanent council on Thursday and unlikely to intervene personally again until the Albanians reached a settlement.

Vranitzky's statement did not specify what consequences Albania would face if its politicians failed to reach a pact, but an OSCE official said it most likely meant a withdrawal of assistance by the OSCE and other international organisations.
"The message is 'We have done all that you have asked us to. Now it's up to you and we're serious'," the official said.
The parties cannot agree on the number of seats to be elected directly or through proportional representation.

Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen of Denmark, the current OSCE chairman, has warned that failure to broker an accord could lead the 54-nation body and other international organisations to end their aid to the former Stalinist state.
Italy, leading a multinational force protecting aid deliveries in Albania, and Greece on Tuesday added their voices to appeals for a quick election agreement.
The multinational protection force is acting under a three-month mandate given by the U.N. Security Council, which is likely to be extended if the elections go ahead.

"The international community is united in its conviction that free and fair elections, involving all parties and sectors of society, are the only solution to the continuing political, economic and security crisis facing Albania," Vranitzky said.

The OSCE, the European Union, the Council of Europe and other bodies pledged to help Albania restructure its political and financial institutions following widespread anarchy across the Balkan state in March, sparked by the collapse of shady pyramid investment schemes.
An OSCE source said that the fact that all organisations were united in their determination to see early elections on June 29 meant Albania could lose more than just political face.
"The fact the EU is involved is significant as part of the project is dealing with economic rehabilitation," he said.
Vranitzky said the international community had shown its effectiveness in building security through cooperation.
"It is now up to the Albanians themselves to take a similarly constructive approach and reach an immediate compromise on the election law," he said.
